overview: This ninth-century map label points to Norway and Iceland, within a much wider Viking-age world of farming, trade, migration and raiding. Its two shaded areas do not represent one securely bounded kingdom. Iceland’s settlers came from Scandinavia and the British Isles; the shading does not establish settlement throughout the entire century. Their households and institutions continued to develop after this imported record stops in 900.

periods.title: Ships, trade and settlement
periods.summary: Norwegian communities participated in Viking-age networks while settlement expanded into Iceland.

periods.title: Later institutions and written traces
periods.summary: Iceland’s assembly and an eleventh-century Norwegian inscription illuminate developments after the map’s ninth-century window.

sections.title: A burial full of everyday equipment

items.text: At Oseberg in Norway, a ship burial contained the remains of two women. The chamber’s timber dates the burial to 834, and excavation began in 1904. Its remarkable preservation lets researchers study objects that usually rot away, alongside the people for whom this elaborate funeral was arranged.

The Oseberg grave included beds, a chair, wooden chests and bedding with down and feathers. Four sledges and a wagon joined the ship. These were possessions selected for a grand burial, so they reveal wealthy material life rather than the furniture budget of every family.

Cooking equipment at Oseberg included two iron cauldrons, one supplied with a stand. There were also three whisk-like tools and five ladles of different sizes. Even a spectacular ship burial preserves the practical business of stirring, scooping and getting dinner out of the pot.

A milk strainer and a rotary quern were also found at Oseberg. The quern consists of two circular stones and retained its turning handle. Grinding grain into flour required repeated physical work; the equipment helps us picture the labor behind food rather than only the feast itself.

sections.title: A town and new homes across the sea

items.text: Kaupang beside the Viksfjord was established around 800. Vestfold Museums estimates that 400 to 600 people may have lived there during the ninth century. Its central area was divided into plots, creating a small, organized settlement along a shoreline that stood higher than today’s.

Cut pieces of amber and unfinished amber beads found at Kaupang suggest that an amber worker operated there. Half-made objects are especially revealing: they show where someone was producing things, rather than simply where a finished necklace was worn or lost.

In Reykjavík, archaeologists uncovered an early wall dated to around 871 north of a later longhouse. This fragment is material evidence of early settlement beneath the modern city. The museum preserves the archaeology where it was found, giving an old wall a very new roof.

The nearby longhouse was inhabited around 930 to 1000, after this map record’s endpoint. Excavation took place before new construction at Aðalstræti and Túngata. Keeping the building’s foundations visible makes it possible to explore a home’s layout without pretending we know the names of its residents.

Around 930, Icelanders established the general assembly at Þingvellir, meaning Assembly Plains. The Law Rock and Law Council became central parts of its work. This later institution provided a place to make decisions and resolve disputes as the island’s communities developed beyond the first settlement generations.

During the Commonwealth period, people gathered at Þingvellir for two weeks each summer. Reaching it could mean days of riding; from the farthest eastern districts the journey could take seventeen days. Surviving booth remains recall the temporary accommodation needed for this major gathering.

Writing sample: “Nóregi” means “Norway.” NTNU prints this normalized Latin-letter form of a word on the Kuli runestone. The original was carved in runes; this is a scholarly rendering rather than a facsimile of the signs. The stone belongs to the eleventh century, later than the map’s 800 to 900 window.

The Kuli Stone combined a carved cross with a runic message about Christianity. It reached the museum in 1913, but its faint runes were rediscovered by curator Aslak Liestøl in 1956. A familiar museum object could still hold overlooked writing waiting for someone to look again.

ending.text: The map’s 900 cutoff is not the end of these communities. Iceland developed the Commonwealth and its assembly; the wider Viking period continued into the eleventh century. New institutions and religious practices changed societies whose households and languages carried on.
